      14. Groups#

      Many counting problems count objects up to some transformations. For example, we can ask how many ways there are to make a round bracelet with beads, each black or red. Turning a bracelet does not change it, so two arrangements that differ by a rotation are the same bracelet. In Figure 1, reading the beads counterclockwise from the marked bead gives black, red, black, red on the left, and black, red, black, red, black on the right; turning the left bracelet by two beads produces the right one.

      To count such quantities efficiently, we need a precise language for the transformations themselves. The algebraic notion that encodes transformations is called a group.

      After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

      • State what a group is, and recognize groups of transformations.

      • Describe every symmetry of a regular -gon as , and compute products using the relations and .

      • Describe the symmetric group of permutations of objects, and analyze the cycle structure of its elements.

      • Explain what a presentation of a group is, and the difficulties involved in studying a group given by a presentation.

      • Compose and invert permutations given by tables, and write permutations in cycle notation.

      • Compose overlapping cycles, and compute conjugates of permutations by relabeling.

      • Decide whether a subset of a finite group is a subgroup, and compute the order of an element.

      • Find the cyclic subgroup generated by an element, relate its size to the order of the element, and decide whether a group is cyclic.

      14.1 Coloring the corners of a square#

      We start with a smaller version of the bracelet problem, coloring the four corners of a square, and identify the properties of the rotations that the solution uses.

      We label the corners of a square counterclockwise, starting at the bottom left, and color each corner black or white. A coloring is recorded by the string of the colors of corners ; for example, BWWW colors corner black and the other three corners white. Each of the four corners has two possible colors, so by the product rule there are colorings.

      Suppose now that the square is a tile lying on a table, with its corners painted, and that the tile can be turned. Turning the tile by counterclockwise carries the paint on corner to the place of corner , the paint on corner to the place of corner , the paint on corner to the place of corner , and the paint on corner to the place of corner . In terms of strings, each letter moves one place to the right and the last letter moves to the front: BWWW becomes WBWW. We regard two colorings as the same up to rotation if one of the four rotations, by , , , or , carries one coloring to the other.

      To find all colorings that are the same as a given one, we apply the rotation repeatedly until we return to the starting coloring. For example, These four colorings form one class. Figure 2 sorts all colorings into classes in this way.

      We describe the classes by the number of black corners.

      • No black corners: WWWW is unchanged by every rotation, so its class has coloring.

      • One black corner: the black corner can be carried to any of the corners, so the class has colorings.

      • Two black corners that are adjacent, that is, joined by a side: the black pair can be carried to any of the sides, so the class has colorings.

      • Two black corners that are opposite: the black pair is one of the diagonals. The half turn carries BWBW to itself, so the class has only colorings.

      • Three black corners: the white corner can be any of the corners, so the class has colorings.

      • Four black corners: BBBB is unchanged by every rotation, so its class has coloring.

      Every coloring appears in exactly one class, and indeed So there are colorings of the corners of a square up to rotation.

      Notice that is the wrong answer: the classes do not all have elements, because some colorings are unchanged by some rotations. Counting classes of different sizes without listing them is the subject of the next lecture note.

      Calling these sets classes makes a claim: the colorings split into sets of colorings that are the same up to rotation, and no coloring lies in two different sets. This claim depends on three properties of the four rotations.

      • Every coloring is the same as itself, because the rotation by changes nothing.

      • If a rotation carries the coloring to , then the rotation by the opposite angle carries back to . So ``the same up to rotation’’ does not depend on the order in which the two colorings are named.

      • If one rotation carries to and another carries to , then performing the two rotations in succession is again one of the four rotations, and it carries to .

      The third property shows that the class found by repeated rotation of BBWW contains every coloring that can be reached from BBWW, and the second shows that every member of that class finds the same class. Thus the classes are well defined because the rotations contain the ``do nothing’’ rotation, contain the reverse of each rotation, and are closed under performing one rotation after another. These are the properties that define a group.

      14.2 Groups#

      The rotations of the square rearrange its corners, so we describe them as permutations. A permutation of a finite set is a bijection . For permutations and of , the composition is the permutation so is applied first. The identity is defined by , and the inverse sends back to . The rotation of the square by counterclockwise is the permutation of with since the corner in place is carried to the place of corner , and corner to the place of corner . The four rotations are , , , and .

      Definition 1 (Group)#

      A group is a set together with an operation that assigns to every an element , such that

      1. (associativity) for all ;

      2. (identity) there is an element with for all ;

      3. (inverses) for every there is an element with .

      The number of elements is the order of .

      The requirement that lie in is the closure property used for the colorings; the identity and inverses are the other two properties. For sets of permutations with composition, associativity holds automatically: and both equal . So a set of permutations of is a group under composition exactly when it contains , contains the inverse of each of its elements, and contains the composition of any two of its elements.

      • The set of all permutations of , with composition. Its order is . We study it in Section 14.5.

      • , where is defined as the remainder of on division by . The identity is , and the inverse of is .

      14.3 The symmetries of a regular polygon#

      Let , and label the corners of a regular -gon counterclockwise. We compute with corner labels modulo , so that means corner and means corner . Two corners are adjacent if they are joined by a side; the corners adjacent to are and . A rotation or reflection that carries the polygon onto itself preserves distances, so it sends adjacent corners to adjacent corners. We use this as the definition.

      Definition 4 (Symmetries of a regular polygon)#

      A symmetry of the regular -gon is a permutation of such that and are adjacent whenever and are adjacent. The set of symmetries, with composition, is the dihedral group .

      The set is a group: the composition of two maps that preserve adjacency preserves adjacency, does, and so does the inverse of a symmetry, because a symmetry sends the adjacent pairs to different adjacent pairs, so its inverse sends them back to adjacent pairs.

      Where can a symmetry send the corners? The next proposition says that only two pieces of information matter: where corner goes, and whether the images of the corners run counterclockwise or clockwise.

      14.4 Presentations#

      A table listing all products quickly becomes impractical: already has products. The previous section suggests a shorter description. A word in and is a string of these letters, such as , and it stands for the composition of the corresponding symmetries. Every element of is given by some word, and we found three relations These relations are enough to compute every product. Applying once for each factor gives , so each can be moved to the right of each . Then removes pairs of ’s and reduces the exponent of to one of . Every word therefore reduces to one of the normal forms .

      Example 6 (Reducing words)#

      In , , as we found from the tables. In , the word reduces as follows. First , so using in the last step. The result has the form , so it is a reflection.

      We record such a description as a presentation, listing the generators and then the relations: In the same way and .

      In general, a presentation describes the group whose elements are words in the generators and their inverses, where two words represent the same element exactly when one can be transformed into the other by inserting or deleting a relation from , or a pair or . We do not need the formal construction of this group. A presentation can be finite even when the group is not; for example, , with no relations, describes the integers under addition. For we could decide when two words are equal because we found normal forms. For a general presentation no such procedure exists.

      Theorem (Undecidability for presentations)#

      There is no algorithm that, given a finite presentation and a word in its generators, decides whether the word equals the identity (Novikov 1955, Boone 1958). Consequently, there is no algorithm that, given two finite presentations, decides whether they define the same group; even deciding whether a presentation defines the group with one element is impossible (Adian 1957, Rabin 1958).

      These results are proved by building presentations that simulate Turing machines, in the same spirit as the undecidability of the halting problem; the proofs are beyond this course. For a finite group given by explicit permutations, these questions can be decided by checking finitely many cases. This is one reason why, for counting, we work with explicit groups of permutations.

      14.5 The symmetric group#

      The symmetries of a polygon are those permutations of its corners that preserve adjacency. Dropping that condition and allowing every permutation of objects gives the largest group of permutations of an -element set.

      Definition 7 (Symmetric group)#

      The symmetric group is the set of all permutations of , with composition. It has elements.

      is a group because the composition of two bijections is a bijection, the identity is a bijection, and the inverse of a bijection is a bijection; associativity holds for compositions, as we saw in Section 14.2.       14.6 Cycle notation#

      Listing the cycles of a permutation describes it completely and shows at once how it moves the elements, so we use the cycles as the standard way to write permutations.

      Definition 9 (Cycle notation)#

      In cycle notation a permutation is written by listing its cycles, each in parentheses: means , , , , and . A cycle with elements is an -cycle, and a -cycle is a transposition.

      The permutation above is . A cycle of length is a fixed point: it does not move anything, so cycles of length are usually omitted, and we write . Every element not listed is understood to be fixed, and the identity is written . Because Theorem 8 lets a cycle start at any of its elements, , , and are the same cycle; but is a different cycle, sending . Reading a cycle backwards gives the inverse: .

      We write for the number of cycles of , including the fixed points. The list of the lengths of the cycles, including the fixed points and written in decreasing order, is the cycle type of . The permutation above has and cycle type . In cycle notation, the eight symmetries of the square are So , , , and ; for instance, has the cycles , , and . This number will count colorings in the next lecture note: a coloring is unchanged by exactly when it is constant on each cycle of .

      Each cycle is itself a permutation, which moves the elements of the cycle and fixes all others. Cycle notation such as can therefore also be read as a composition of three permutations. The two readings agree, and the order in which the cycles are written does not matter, because of the following fact. Two cycles are disjoint if they have no element in common.

      When two cycles share an element, Proposition 10 does not apply, and the product usually cannot be read off from the factors. The only reliable method is to follow each element through the factors from right to left. Both are -cycles, although the factors are a -cycle and a transposition, so even the cycle type of a product cannot be read from the cycle types of overlapping factors. A common error is to apply the left factor first; in this example that error turns one answer into the other.

      14.9 Cyclic groups#

      The rotation group consists of the powers of the single rotation , and every element of is obtained by adding to itself repeatedly. Groups built from one element in this way are the simplest groups, and the number of elements they contain turns out to be the order of that element.

      Definition 21 (Cyclic subgroup)#

      Let be an element of a finite group . The cyclic subgroup generated by is the set of all powers of , with positive, zero, and negative exponents.

      The definition lists infinitely many powers, but in a finite group only finitely many of them are different, and the order of tells us exactly how many.

      14.10 Cayley’s theorem#

      Every finite group is isomorphic to a permutation group. The permutations come from the group itself: each element rearranges the elements of by multiplication on the left.
